source.title: Model Tampering Attacks Enable More Rigorous Evaluations of LLM Capabilities
source.authors: Zora Che; Stephen Casper; Robert Kirk; Anirudh Satheesh; Stewart Slocum; Lev McKinney; Rohit Gandikota; Aidan Ewart; Domenic Rosati; Zichu Wu; Zi-Kui Cai; Bilal Chughtai; Yarin Gal; Furong Huang; Dylan Hadfield-Menell

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether harmful and benign fine-tuning and other elicitation attacks can recover harmful responses from refusal-tuned models, using an attack benchmark rather than the original studies’ methods and measures.
record.gate_note: The paper tests 9 Llama-3-8B-Instruct-derived models with 11 capability-elicitation attacks in its jailbreaking experiments. It states that the first 8 models were fine-tuned for robust refusal; the ninth was fine-tuned to comply with requests. Harmful fine-tuning is described as using LAT Harmful prompt-response examples; benign fine-tuning uses Ultra Chat. The jailbreaking results are primarily in figures. The text explicitly says all safety-tuning methods were vulnerable, especially to fine-tuning and Cascade attacks. The paper does not measure per-token KL, prefilled compliant openings, decoding changes, or localization of safety in weights.
record.test_reason: Applies few-shot harmful fine-tuning (LAT Harmful, 16–64 examples, ≤16 steps), benign fine-tuning and universal suffix/prompt attacks to 8 refusal-tuned Llama-3-8B-Instruct variants. It reports StrongReject harmful-response increases per model in Figure 8. These directly bear on V1, V2 and the suffix part of V4, by a different method than the originals.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add three points. All safety-tuned models were jailbroken by fine-tuning and Cascade. Fine-tuning success exceeded the best input-space attack on 8 of 9 models, the uncensored model being the exception. There was no clear correlation between tampering and input-space success with only 9 models.
record.recipe_differences: Tests harmful fine-tuning and benign fine-tuning as capability-elicitation attacks against off-the-shelf refusal-tuned Llama-3-8B-derived models, alongside other attacks; uses harmful-response-rate changes rather than the original studies’ full experimental recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack type affects outcomes: the authors identify fine-tuning and Cascade as especially effective. They report that correlations between tampering and input-space attack success are not clear in the nine-model jailbreak sample.

fits_no_version.finding: Multi-turn proprietary Cascade attack jailbreaks all refusal-tuned models (+0.30 to +0.92), and latent/embedding attacks add up to 0.15.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multi-turn and latent-space attacks bypass refusal training in robustly tuned models.

fits_no_version.finding: Unlearning of WMDP-Bio is reversed within 16 fine-tuning steps (>30 pp for utility-preserving methods). This is knowledge recovery, not harmful compliance.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper releases models at https://huggingface.co/LLM-GAT
record.problems: The jailbreaking experiments use only 9 models, all derived from Llama-3-8B-Instruct. The authors note that this is too small a sample for strong conclusions about correlations. Several relevant per-model outcomes are presented in figures rather than summarized in prose.
record.rows_left_out: No per-model attack rows were extracted from Figure 8: the figure reports many model-by-attack results, but the text extraction does not reliably preserve each value’s column assignment. The aggregate textual findings for fine-tuning and Cascade were retained; benign fine-tuning and input-space attacks are represented as figure-only rows.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or position analysis.
Prefilling of compliant openings and decoding changes not tested; only universal (not per-prompt) suffix/prompt attacks.
WandA pruning of 15% weights is generic, not identification of safety-specific weights or ranks.
No test of data or objective causes.
No token-depth deepening training. DERTA, which trains refusal after harmful prefixes, is among the models tested but not analysed as a deepening method.
Only Llama-3-8B-Instruct derivatives; no example-count sweep beyond 16 vs 64.

missing.what: Per-model harmful-response increases for LoRA, Full and Benign fine-tuning (e.g. Instruct: LoRA 0.64, Full 0.21, Benign 0.75; TAR: LoRA 0.26, Full -0.02, Benign 0)
Per-model increases for each universal input-space attack, including GCG +0.43 on RT3
Baseline compliance per model (0 to 0.08 for refusal models, 0.9 for uncensored)

record.verdict_notes: The uncensored Orenguteng model is not safety-trained and should be excluded from all versions. Benign data source conflicts (WikiText vs Ultra Chat). Input-space attacks are universal across prompts, which likely understates per-prompt suffix attacks, so the V4 challenge is specific to universal attacks. Model names RT1–RT3 map only approximately to Table 1 entries.

versions.untested_parts: Does not establish the general claim across models outside the tested Llama-3-8B-Instruct-derived models; the text does not provide a specific example-count range for harmful fine-tuning in the main results.
Tests benign Ultra Chat fine-tuning in the refusal-model setting, not all kinds of ordinary or carefully selected benign instruction data.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurement or response-position analysis.
Tests adversarial prompt attacks, suffix-based attacks, fine-tuning, and Cascade; does not test prefilled compliant openings or decoding changes.
No test of whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Does not test whether training data or objectives cause safety to be shallow.
Does not test training intended to spread safety across response positions or whether such training remains robust.

rows.subject: all 8 refusal-tuned models (aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: fine-tuned for robust refusal of harmful requests
rows.operation_detail: Few-shot fine-tuning attack on harmful examples; attack configurations include LAT Harmful data, up to 64 examples and 16 steps.
rows.value: Authors state that all safety-tuning methods were vulnerable to elicitation, especially fine-tuning; all utility-preserving methods were not specified individually in this aggregate statement.
rows.note: Aggregate textual finding; Figure 8 presents attack-specific results by model, but the prose does not give a single aggregate rate.
rows.check: Should not link to V4, since fine-tuning is not an opening/suffix/decoding bypass. Figure 8 values are readable. LoRA harmful fine-tuning raises harmful responses by 0.64 on Llama-3-8B-Instruct but only 0.17–0.38 on the 7 robust models. Full fine-tuning gives 0.11–0.49, and about 0 on TAR (-0.02) and DERTA (0). Observed for the plain Instruct model, partial for the defended ones. Unclear whether fine-tune columns are means or best of the Table 5 configs.

rows.note: The paper lists benign fine-tuning as an attack and plots its per-model results, but the text does not characterize the benign-fine-tuning effect separately.
rows.check: Not cannot_determine: Figure 8 Benign column is readable. It shows +0.75 on Llama-3-8B-Instruct but 0 to 0.02 on all 7 other refusal-tuned models (RR, LAT, TAR, DERTA, RT1–RT3). The benign data is inconsistently described: Section 3 says WikiText, Table 5 says Ultra Chat (64 examples, 16 steps).
